topic: nvidia preps to sell vera cpus into china amid gpu sales freeze
headline_marked: Nvidia [[preps Vera CPU sales]] in China as GPU shipments remain frozen
headline: Nvidia preps Vera CPU sales in China as GPU shipments remain frozen
summary: Nvidia is reportedly encouraging Chinese clients to place orders for its Arm-based Vera server CPUs, with shipments potentially starting as early as August. This comes as H200 AI GPU sales to China are still on hold.
details: Nvidia has informed Chinese clients that its Arm-based Vera server CPUs could be available as soon as August, with orders being accepted now, according to Reuters citing three sources. This move occurs while shipments of Nvidia's H200 AI GPUs to China remain frozen, months after CEO Jensen Huang stated Nvidia's market share in the country had effectively dropped to zero.

This August timeline aligns with indications given at GTC Taipei during Computex, where Nvidia suggested Vera systems would reach customers through system builders and cloud partners in the fall. The company expects the Vera CPU line to generate $20 billion in revenue by the end of its fiscal year in late January, indicating its strategic importance.

Chinese cloud companies are reportedly already testing over 300 Vera servers overseas, with at least one major provider planning to place an order. Initial deployments will be confined to these companies' international data centers, as server CPUs face significantly lighter U.S. export restrictions compared to AI accelerators.

The U.S. government has placed stringent restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China, impacting Nvidia's GPU business. Despite the U.S. licensing roughly 10 Chinese firms to purchase the H200 GPU, no units have been delivered due to China's own withholding of approval, aimed at nurturing domestic chipmakers.

This situation explains the restriction of Vera CPU deployments to overseas data centers. While Chinese cloud providers are eager for the hardware, integrating U.S. silicon into domestic data centers could attract scrutiny from Beijing officials. Vera CPUs began as part of the Vera Rubin superchip and were later spun off as a standalone product.

Nvidia launched the standalone Vera CPU at GTC San Jose in March, alongside a rack design capable of housing 256 liquid-cooled Vera CPUs. The company claimed the chip offers 1.8 times faster task completion than x86 processors on agentic workloads, and its predecessor, Grace, has shipped nearly 2.5 million units.

The server CPU market is currently experiencing high demand due to the shift of AI workloads from training to inference and agentic execution. Agentic AI relies heavily on host processors for tasks like tool calls, code execution, and data handling, leading to a CPU supply shortage.

Both Intel and AMD are facing significant demand for their server CPUs, with Intel quoting lead times of up to six months for Chinese customers. AMD has also noted that the global CPU market is tight, with demand exceeding forecasts and supply constraints expected to continue.
